title: Role of PLVAP in Glomerular Endothelial Cell Injury
text:
Injury to glomerular endothelial cells (GEnCs) is a common feature across the wide spectrum of glomerular
diseases and its severity directly correlates with loss of glomerular filtration rate (GFR), however despite this,
mechanisms of GEnC response to injury are poorly understood due to their highly unique structure and function.
Healthy, mature GEnCs lack expression of Plasmalemma vesicle-associated protein (Plvap), the only known
component of diaphragms that span fenestrations and caveolae, which is contrary to all other systemic
fenestrated endothelial beds, and interestingly both Plvap and Cav-1, the key scaffolding protein of caveolae,
are upregulated in GEnC injury. This proposal will elucidate the regulation and pathogenic role of PLVAP and its
associated structures—fenestral diaphragms and caveolae—in GEnCs within the context of TMA, with the long-
term goal of uncovering novel mechanistic insights into GEnC pathobiology.

title: Exploiting time-of-flight in photon cascade emissions for direct imaging of therapeutic radionuclides
text:
(Relevance)
Nuclear imaging is extremely important to diagnose cancer and monitor cancer progression and treatment.
Currently, an imaging technology capable of delivering quality images of cancer radionuclide therapy is
unavailable. In this project, we will establish a new imaging technique intended to provide efficient and accurate
images of the most popular drugs used in this cancer treatment modality.

title: Co-transmission of GABA and Glutamate in Cortical Circuits.
text: Project Narrative. Neuromodulators powerfully influence neural activity and facilitate plasticity, but their sites of action within complex neural circuits are not well understood. This proposal will characterize a unique cortical neuron that is a key target for the neuromodulators serotonin and acetylcholine and that co-releases both the excitatory neurotransmitter, glutamate, and the inhibitory neurotransmitter, GABA. We envision that the results of this research will identify novel therapeutic targets for mental disorders that tap into specific synaptic and cellular mechanisms to modulate adult cortical processing and promote plasticity.

title: Spontaneous and Induced B cell and T cell responses in Alzheimer's Disease
text:
The US FDA recently approved aducanumab, an antibody that promotes clearance of Aβ plaques in patients
with Alzheimer's disease, and other antibodies are currently tested in patients to remove brain aggregates of
Tau, another protein causing Alzheimer's disease. Here we propose to study whether Alzheimer's disease
patients and mouse models develop natural antibodies and immune responses against Aβ and Tau aggregates,
whether these responses correlate with disease progression and whether their presence can help identify
patients that will benefit from antibody therapy.

title: DNA Damage Response and Oncogenic Signaling
text: To support the development of novel anti-cancer therapies, we propose continuation of a multidisciplinary, institution-wide cancer biology T32 postdoctoral training program at City of Hope (Duarte, CA) to prepare exceptionally motivated postdoctoral fellows in the fields of DNA damage response and oncogenic signaling (DNADRS). We have implemented a comprehensive strategy, which is aided by exceptional institutional support for salaries and research funds, to emphasize attracting and training scientists that show promise in securing independent cancer research positions within academia and in the biotechnology sector. With our collection of outstanding DNADRS researchers and physician collaborators, state of the art facilities, strong curriculum, emphasis on obtaining extramural funding, superb institutional support, and the last 5 years’ successful experience, we request the continued support to DNADRS T32 program, which will train the next generation of leaders in the fight against cancer.

title: Probing mechanisms of long QT type 2-associated neuronal dysfunction using gene-edited stem cell-derived neurons
text:
Patients with mutations in a protein called hERG1 develop epilepsy at a greater rate than the
general population, but we don't know why. In this project we will study brain cells grown from
patients with hERG1 mutations and compare them to brain cells grown from healthy individuals.
This will allow us to identify mechanisms by which hERG1 mutations change brain cell behavior
to promote epilepsy.

title: Novel mechanisms regulating PD-1 signaling and function
text:
Cancer immunotherapies represent a powerful therapeutic paradigm because they are applicable to a wide variety of
tumors and can produce durable clinical responses; however, only a fraction of patients experience clinical benefit from
current immunotherapies, and as such there is an urgent need to develop new therapies. Our studies will focus on the
immune cells underlying the resistance to current immunotherapies. Uncovering novel aspects of the immune system is
crucial not just for better understanding the biology of the immune response to tumor, but also for designing the next
generation therapeutics.

title: Elucidating Mechanisms and Design Principles for Chemically Inducible Expression Modulation
text:
While expression engineering tools have great potential to enhance fundamental science and medicine, the lack
of effective ways to control their activity limits their utility. We aim to generate a deeper understanding of
transduction mechanisms that could fill this need and use these insights to design better expression control tools.

title: Compartmental, rhythmic and plastic neuropeptide release
text:
This project will elucidate mechanisms that regulate neuropeptide packaging and release from terminals
undergoing plasticity and the soma, a noncanonical site of release. These mechanisms are essential to
understanding how neuropeptides control rhythmic behaviors (e.g., circadian rhythms and sleep), pain,
appetite, and mood.

title: Hypothalamic lipid signaling in metabolism regulation
text:
To understand the etiology of metabolic disorders and motivated behavior it is essential that we gain
better insight into the neuronal mechanisms that regulate metabolism and behavior. We propose studies that
will assess and define the role of lipid metabolism in the arcuate melanocortin neurons in the regulation
of feeding behavior and energy metabolism.
The proposed studies are a logical continuation of our ongoing studies and, if successful, their completion will
unmask a novel mechanistic principle in central regulation of feeding and systemic metabolism.

title: miR-10b Gene Editing Therapy for Glioblastoma
text:
Glioblastoma (GBM) is one the most lethal forms of cancer and represents a significant unmet need
in current medicine. We identified miR-10b, essential for glioma growth, as a top and common
therapeutic target for GBM. This project will develop miR-10b-gene editing therapy for a “first-in-
human” clinical trial on GBM.

title: Development and application of new tools to identify repeat expansions in human diseases
text:
The proposed research is relevant to public health because it will enable the identification of pathogenic repeat
expansions in human disease, leading to a new class of precision-targeted therapeutics. The proposed
research is relevant to NHGRI because new genomic tools are urgently needed to identify these repeat
expansions.

title: Human Factors of Aging Program
text:
(Include Public Health Relevance) (Three sentences)
Public Health Relevance: Research often leads to ideas that can be translated to new devices, interventions
and programs, particularly in aging. Understanding and implementing fundamental human factors principles
and practice are critical to effective and successful translation. The Human Factors of Aging Program is
designed to meet this need for researchers, clinicians and students who wish to have a positive impact on the
lives of older adults through innovation and translation.

title: Understanding Early Development of the Human Placenta: A Crucial Step Toward Solving the Preeclampsia Puzzle.
text:
Preeclampsia is a human-specific disease of pregnancy characterized by incomplete growth and invasion of
the placenta into the uterus. Little is known about human placental development strategies and implantation,
given that the initiation of this process occurs during a time frame that is completely concealed in humans. My
lab will utilize stem cell models to reconstruct early placental villi in vitro, and as a result of these studies, we
aim to develop therapies for pregnancy-related diseases such as preeclampsia.

title: Development of Adipose Derived Stems Cells System for HCMV latency
text:
Human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) establishes lifelong latency and poses a serious threat
to immunocompromised individuals and newborns, yet current therapies are limited by
toxicity and resistance. This project will evaluate adipose-derived stem cells (ADSCs) as
a novel, physiologically relevant model for studying HCMV latency and its transcriptional
regulation. A better understanding of HCMV latency mechanisms could enable the
development of targeted therapies to prevent viral reactivation and reduce disease
burden in vulnerable populations.

title: Antigen immunodominance in regulation of anti-tumor CD8 T cell immunity and immunotherapy response
text:
Cancer immunotherapies that activate killer T cells against tumors are highly effective at eradicating cancer, but
only in a subset of patients. We have shown that T cell activity against tumors is limited by a phenomenon called
antigen immunodominance that causes T cells to respond to only one or a few tumor antigens out of up to
hundreds. This project will elucidate the mechanisms underlying antigen immunodominance in tumors and test
therapeutic strategies to overcome it and promote broader and more effective T cell responses against cancer.

title: High Throughput Screening Facility
text: PROJECT SUMMARY/ABSTRACT – SHARED RESOURCE: HIGH THROUGHPUT SCREENING FACILITY The High Throughput Screening Facility (HTSF) provides screening platforms and specialized instrumentation for increased experimental throughput to support the research of FCCC members. The HTSF provides the capability to perform hypothesis-generating discovery research with the major goal of generating insights that can be pre-clinically and clinically advanced. Beyond the context of screening, the HTSF works with individual investigators to perform assay development and execute specific projects requiring wet-bench capacity, which increasingly include correlate studies for FCCC clinical trials. In support of these functions, the HTSF provides access to specialized equipment, expertise, and direct services that enable investigators to address novel areas of translational research that would be difficult or impossible to pursue without the liquid handling, assay resources, reagents and experience of the HTSF. Specifically, the HTSF provides the liquid handling (CyBio- Well Vario, Matrix Wellmate, BioTek Precision XS, Tecan D300e), assay instrumentation platforms (Perkin Elmer Envision multilabel plate reader, Guava EasyCyte, ImageXpress Micro confocal automated imaging and analysis, BioPlex 100/200) and libraries (small molecule: ChemDiv Diverse, ICCB known Bioactives, Johns Hopkins Clinical Compound Collection, custom targeted collections; RNAi: Horizon Discovery whole genome and targeted subsets; and CRISPR: whole genome human and mouse KO libraries) to enable FCCC members to add these experimental approaches to their research programs. The HTSF has been directed by Golemis (CSM) for the past 15 years, and has one FTE, the Facility Manager Einarson (CSM), who has led day to day operations since facility’s inception in 2005. This team possess the expertise to support users via assay design, development and execution. From 2019-2023 (October) 41 FCCC members across all three Research Programs utilized the HTSF. In the 12 months ending 10/31/23, there were 23 users from all three research programs, with peer-review funded FCCC members logging 99% of the usage hours on instrumentation. Recent addition to the instrumentation in the HTSF includes the purchase of a dual wide-field confocal automated microscope (IXM-C, Molecular Devices) and Tecan D300e. Institutional investment in equipment since 2019 totaled $351,023. Additional institutional investments in compound and CRISPR libraries have further expanded capabilities. Specific aims of the HTSF are to provide professional support for the instrumentation and libraries necessary to perform high throughput screening, to enable investigators to utilize individual instruments for experimentation involving limited analytes/samples and multiplexed readouts, and to work one-on-one with FCCC members to develop assays to target cancer-relevant questions. Oversight of the HTSF is provided by a Facility Advisory Committee (FAC) that meets at least annually. Recommendations from the FAC are directed to a governing Facility Parent Oversight Committee that ensures that the HTSF continues to have resources necessary to provide the highest quality services for FCCC members.

title: AstroPath Integration Resource Core
text: The AstroPath-Genomics Core will be a hub to disseminate powerful molecular pathology, informatics, big data science, and genomics methods tailored to accomplish the goals of the Prostate TBEL Program. It will provide critical support for ALL three projects. The key strategy is to leverage existing infrastructure, equipment and services at the SKCCC, while also providing specialized approaches and capabilities that are highly tailored to support the activities in the TBEL Program. This model will allow efficient and cost-effective harnessing of these powerful technologies through the dedicated effort and expertise of the current AstroPath-Genomics Core personnel through the close interaction with all Projects and Cores here, without having to establish the equipment, administrative infrastructure, biospecimen SOPs, and laboratory informatics management systems (LIMS), from scratch. This centralization of the molecular pathology, informatics and big data science, and mathematical/computational integration methods will yield cost-effective strategies that avoid duplicating effort in each component of the TBEL Program. The Core will carry out its work in three major Aims. Aim 1 will deploy advanced digital pathology tools for multi-analyte immunohistochemistry, immunofluorescence, and in situ hybridization approaches and image analysis for deep characterization of the microenvironmental transitions from inflammation to neoplasia. Specific technologies include multi-spectral multi-analyte imaging, Chromogenic iterative multiplex-IHC(ChIM-IHC), and multiplex ACD in situ hybridization. Aim 2 will utilize bulk, single cell, and spatial genomics approaches to measure the genomic and epigenomic alterations to the epithelial and stromal compartments of PIA, PIN, and cancer lesions. Specific technologies include, genome wide and ultra-deep targeted DNA methylation analysis, multi-modal single nucleus ATAC- and coupled RNA- seq (snATAC-/snRNA-seq), and spatial transcriptomics. Integration across the multi-modal data streams will be possible through implementation of the innovative Bayesian non-negative matrix factorization and transfer learning approaches through the CoGAPS and ProjectR framework. Aim 3 will implement and extend the AstroPath framework for computational analysis of high dimensional single cell and bulk genomics/epigenomics, multi-analyte digital pathology, and advanced imaging data. To accomplish these goals, the core leaders have assembled an impressive team of experts to support the TBEL Center, with complementary expertise in big data science/informatics, molecular pathology, genomics technologies, immunopathology, computational/systems biology and applied mathematics.

title: Translational Research Training Program in Environmental Health Sciences
text:
This T32 Training Program is dedicated to the training of the next generation of environmental health
scientists by emphasizing training in translational research that transcends basic and population based
research, patient oriented research, community engagement and public health policy.
